blocks.x: I was saying one of the greatest things that I remember from communicating with Cannonball Adler, he told me, no matter how great you think you are, there's always a performer that's playing somewhere else, that the people that's experiencing them at the time, if they enjoyed it, they consider that great. So, you know, you can only play in one place at a time, no matter how great you are. So if you let somebody else's greatness determine how you feel about yourself, it's the biggest mistake that you could ever make. And that always stuck with me, you know. Because when you're playing and you have admiration for other people, you sometimes think that they have a greater formula for what's happening. What's happening in their head?

It just depends on the setting. I can play everything from the Little Richards to whatever is fusion to all of that. And I think to a large degree that that has been our problem. People having record companies sometimes want you to have, to market you, they want you to record in one mode. And you know I know personally I can sing, I can sing jazz, I can sing rock and roll, or whatever. And when you're promoting yourself no one wants to hear you blow your horn. And since I've come to that realization I sometimes suppress what my opinions, I mean be kind of careful about where I'll say them, you know, because of how it may be construed. But I certainly think that there's a much broader base and more people that deserve higher recognition. Not just because of what they're doing currently, but because of what they have contributed to the people who sometimes are given credit for being innovators of what's happening now. They've actually taken all of those things from these guys. And I think maybe someday we can come up with a list of people that I think that should be more recognized. I mean there are so many players that have become just frustrated with the way that they've been treated in this town. And you would think with the rise of tourism, I'm on the board of the Black Tourism Center, and I've just been appointed to the Music Commission in New Orleans. And one of the things that I want to push for is higher visibility of guys that'll be selected by people who know, not necessarily people who choose who's the most popular and the most easy to get along with. Because a lot of times a lot of the serious players are shoved in the corner because they don't want to cater to the games that a lot of people want to play with them. Because they've paid the dues. And I know it's a problem because when people are dealing with business, sometimes they don't want the intervention of people who want to stand them up and make them treat them right. Because they have an idea of how to use the music. And hopefully I'll be able to make a difference in the way the Music Commission will start embracing the music. And the idea of the workshop was to create a setting where guys who desired to play modern jazz could play without someone standing over them and trying to dictate where the music would evolve. Because we don't know where the music would evolve if it was not suppressed and controlled by a lot of times non-musical people. And a lot of times some of the answers to frustration and all that comes from the kind of music that we listen to. And you may be depressed and go on and put on a particular record that will just cool you out. And I think radio stations, especially in New Orleans, should take a stronger responsibility as to what kind of music is played. So you know appreciation for a lot of the public broadcast stations, they seem to have a greater sensitivity to playing broader forms of music. And I think that's needed. And when you can develop a different kind of closeness with people who have control over what's marketed, I think a lot of things in this city will change.

Speaking of marketing, would you talk a little bit about the workshop? And I know that there were people, big name musicians, Cannonball Adderley for one, Joe Zawinil for another, who were interested in what you were doing and were here. Would you talk a little bit about that?

Well, fortunately at the time that the workshop happened, Al Hurd had a club on Bourbon Street that featured a lot of the name acts. And when serious musicians come to town, they kind of look for the places to go to hear differently. And we had gotten a pretty good reputation as jazz players. And you know, Freddie Hubbard's just about Jimmy Smith. I can remember meeting all those people in the workshop. And I mean, their main reason for being in this city was them being employed over at Al Hurd's. And then I can remember meeting Milt Jackson. Ray Charles came through the workshop once with Larry McKinley. And bear in mind that, you know, prior to the workshop period, we were pretty popular as, I mean, Willie T and the Souls. We evolved to a jazz band. But we were at one time a serious R&B band, too. I mean, we played all of the music. It just evolved to a point where we wanted to play to discover how far our music could go. And, you know, as a result I got a chance at Cannonball Adderley and Victor Gaskin, Roy McCurtis, all guys who had serious experience in just traveling and knowing the difference in what was great. For them to embrace our music, it was just confirmation that we were going in a better direction. I mean, out of that, my association with Cannonball Adderley, and one of the things that biggest compliments to his music is that Dizzy Glepsey came in and stole my band. And George Davidson and David Lee wound up playing with Dizzy Glepsey's band for years. And, you know, I mean the reason that they left, I know, was economics. You know, I'm sure that Earl has his views as to what happened to the workshop from a business standpoint. And we operated for a long time without a budget. People came and saw us strictly because of the music. I mean, we even had a few colleges that had brought in different groups of people. I think that now would even be a great time to have a place like the workshop where guys could come in and have the freedom to play what they want to play without a club or a standover. Because I think that there is still an audience of people that's just looking for somewhere different to go, that they can hear something that's totally different. So maybe through the commission we'll be able to have some influence on getting people involved in underwriting projects such as that. Even if it's a thing that will happen only for a couple of nights, you know. Especially in a home of jazz. You should be bombarded with modern jazz in New Orleans. It shouldn't just be. And it's not to diminish the value of Dixieland music, but from the time you hit the airport in New Orleans, you should know that you're somewhere totally different. You know. I mean, to come to the home of jazz and to not hear being bombarded with jazz is equivalent to going to China and not having any authentic Chinese food.
And Zawinul became very interested in the kind of music you were playing. Isn't that true?

Zawinul has recorded. Me and Joe Zawinul became real good friends through the years. With as much admiration as I had for Joe's playing, he would come over to my house. And I can honestly say that I've heard some of the things that I played evolve in his music, whether it was conscious or subconscious. And I guess at this point I don't choose to look at it as a negative. At the time that it was happening that day, because I certainly wanted to be recognized for a lot of things that we did. I mean, when you go back to the Mercy Mercies and stuff, and I just wish that I had a copy of the music that we recorded for Canada before that music came out. It would be interesting to just hear the similarities, you know.

Do you remember a little bit about the social and political times that the workshop existed in? I mean, that was a time of the drugs and peace and love, and yet at the same time the civil rights movement and the riots and the black nationalism movement and, you know, the flower children and the hippie world. It was a real interesting time.

Well, what's interesting is that the area in which the workshop was located in was one of those areas where you had a lot of hippies, a lot of bombs and stuff that's just hanging out on the streets. But that didn't, for some reason, the music was such a drawing force that we had all kinds of people that was coming in to experience the music. And I think that no matter what walk of life or what your experience is at some point, your spirit can be fed by what you hear. And certainly we had all kinds of people that were experiencing the workshop, but it didn't, I mean, we had college professors to just guys who were homeless hanging on the street that would come in because they gravitated to the music. And now to just see what has evolved in that area is unreal. One of the major jazz clubs, Durville is right across the street from where the workshop was. And she just points out to me that we were way ahead of our time in terms of that. And I certainly appreciate persons like yourself having the experience and to choose to just give some kind of recognition to what's happening. And I think that that's what's needed more than anything for people outside of the music, per se, to embrace it and to show an interest in it evolving to other levels. And I can't even find the words to tell you how much I appreciate your coming in and supporting us at the time because I can remember seeing you there many times. And, you know, people showing appreciation for what you do just causes you to just dig a little deeper, you know. And I think a lot of people that knew something about the grants and how to go about getting it maybe stole some of the ideas of what this thing was about. And a lot of times you don't get credit for what you influence. But I know that just from hearing the levels of what everybody else plays, that Earl is in my estimation one of the greatest players to ever play a saxophone. But for me sometimes it's hard to accept from someone as close as I am, but all that needs to be done is to have some exposure of what this thing is about. You know, hey.

Do you, did you have anything to do with like the school concept of the workshop? I know that you all had plans to maybe bring in some kids and spend some time with them. Was that more Earl's interest or yours or everybody's?

Well, I think Earl is always gravitated towards sharing the experience of trying to inform people on another level. I mean, Earl would go and play in the prisons. I mean, stuff that a lot of people would shy off from. But you've got to understand that George Davis comes from a serious educational background. And one of the greatest experiences that I've had and the things that I've learned was from my experience of playing with George. I mean, George played with the Juilliard. I mean, he is a much greater musician than most people, I guess, gives him credit for being, or even know that he is. Because George is not only a guitarist, George's major instrument was the flute. And I mean, he played as much as Hubert Laws or anybody that, as much saxophone as anybody that I know. And knows as much as much as just the whole theory and the whole formal aspect of music. I mean, these are people that have a serious background in the music. We just happen to evolve to a point where we wanted to have a freedom of expression that is beyond a particular formula. It's like being in a lab trying to discover the cure for cancer. I mean, sometimes it can come from something that is so totally obscure and from what you would normally do. And I think that's what innovation is. Trying something that is against the norm or against what people might say is the proper way to do it. You know.
Do you have any special, one night that stands out in your mind as very special from the workshop? What is it, Rene?

The one night that I remember more than anything is the night that Ray Charles came to the workshop. I mean, we were playing, they had three levels to the workshop. And sometimes there was like a roof that we would go up and just stand up and when we would take our breaks. And when we came down, Ray Charles was in the audience. And for me, I was such a fan of Ray Charles, just to be able to play and for him to be there and stay as long as he did. It was just such a charge for me. And then to have an opportunity to talk to him on a level that was totally different than you just inspirating him at a concert and trying to get some words in as a fan. And I can remember that. I can remember the nights that Cannon came. And I can vaguely remember, I was trying to say the Roland Kirk, but I remember the experience of Roland Kirk at night at Lewin Charlie's when he was here, which was another institution that stands out in my memory, and it was one of the places that you'd get some recognition too. Because a lot of the guys that were serious players really enjoyed playing there. I can honestly say that the workshop had the biggest influence on me being able to just develop a freer sense of what could happen if you allowed your spirit to just go where it led you. And it helped me to get to the approaches that I have at the music now.
Will you talk just a little bit about the closing of the workshop and the demise of it, and what you recollect from maybe why it closed or those kinds of things?

Well, I think one of the basic reasons that after a while we weren't able to market it as well as we could. I think that maybe if we had more people who had a serious background in writing grants and seeing the need for it, then maybe it would have survived, you know. I think Earl had a closer touch as to what was actually happening with that thing. Because to a large degree this is Earl's baby. I mean, you know, I loved the opportunity to do it, but I certainly don't want to take all the credit for making it happen. We all sort of embraced the idea after Earl initiated the contact with Jules Khan and the people who had the building. And certainly they went along with us for a long period of time of just trying to make it happen. And at some point, you know, when you don't generate enough dollars, then that's what I think at that time there weren't enough people that had sensitivity to the music. Or we weren't able to just market it to a degree where we were getting to those people that knew that such a place existed, in my estimation. It would be interesting to hear what the other people have to say as to what happened.
How do you want the workshop remembered?

I wanted to be remembered as a place that was definitely dedicated to just playing a high, high form of music that had no boundaries, and that wanted to, even with its freedom, to be as enjoyable as any commercial music that people choose to think is what people would want to do. It's what people want to hear. And as a place that made an attempt to give a platform for players to just be able to play whatever they felt. You know, excuse me.
Okay. Is there anything else that we haven't covered that you want to say about the workshop? I mean, we've talked about quite a few things, but...

Well, not really. I mean, I'm sure that when I leave here, I'll probably say, well, that was something else that I could have said. I just hope that through your efforts of bringing this to people's attention, that maybe they will see reason to start plugging into people who are innovators of the music, and may have some different suggestions as to how to make it more appealing to younger players that might want to pursue a higher form of the music, not for their music to be dictated to and suppressed by record companies that are just looking for some formula to make money. I mean, the idea is to make money, but I still think that this music is worth something. And I mean, it's proven. I mean, when you have opportunities to go to Europe and see the difference in the way people accept the art form, that it's just a matter of education and a matter of, I guess, the powers that be to see that we've tried all of the other ways, and maybe this is another way that we could start exploring, and may tend to increase people's interest in tourism and jazz. I mean, it's just the home of jazz.
Brad, do you have anything else you want to add? Hello? Hello?
